I'd say **(A) should be legal**.

Look, I think if people want to use it, that's their choice—similar to alcohol. From what I've seen, legalization in states that have done it hasn't caused the problems people predicted. Plus, there are medical benefits for some folks, and it reduces the burden on the criminal justice system. 

The regulation and tax revenue aspect makes sense to me too. That said, I understand why some people worry about it, especially regarding younger users. But I think that's manageable through regulation rather than outright banning it.

I'd go with **(A) favor**.

Look, I think it makes sense to have some kind of check before someone buys a gun. A permit process gives authorities a chance to verify someone doesn't have a serious criminal history or mental health crisis that would make them a danger. It's similar to needing a license to drive—you're dealing with something that can cause real harm, so some basic screening seems reasonable to me.

I'm not saying the system would be perfect or that it would stop all gun violence, but it seems like a common-sense safety measure. Most people buying guns legally aren't going to have a problem getting a permit anyway.

I'd say **(B) pretty happy**.

Look, life's got ups and downs, you know? I've got things to be grateful for—people I care about, work that keeps me occupied. But there's always something, isn't there? Bills, worries about the future, the general state of things. I'm not going to say I'm "very happy" because that feels like overselling it. But "not too happy" doesn't fit either. I'm managing okay, doing alright most days. That feels like "pretty happy" to me.

I'd say **(B) good**.

I don't have any major health issues that I'm dealing with, and I'm able to do most of the things I want to do. But I'm also realistic—I've got the occasional ache or pain, and I'm not in peak physical condition. So "excellent" feels like overselling it, but "fair" would be underselling it too. Good is about right for where I'm at.

I'd say **(C) depends**.

In my experience, it really varies by situation and who you're dealing with. In my daily life, I see plenty of people being genuinely helpful—neighbors, coworkers, strangers holding doors. But I'd be lying if I said self-interest isn't usually mixed in there somewhere, even if it's just feeling good about helping.

I think most people probably lean toward being helpful when it doesn't cost them much, but when there's real sacrifice involved or their own needs are pressing, that changes things. It's not black and white.

(D) not wrong at all

Look, two consenting adults doing what they choose to do in their private lives—that's their business. I don't see how it hurts anyone else. People should be free to live their lives the way they see fit, as long as everyone involved is a willing adult.

(C) don't know

Look, I can see both sides of this pretty clearly. There's the compassion angle—if someone's suffering terribly and there's no hope, I get why people would want that option. But there's also real concerns about abuse, pressure on vulnerable people, and whether we're abandoning folks too quickly.

It's one of those questions where thoughtful people disagree, and I don't think there's an easy answer. I'd want to know more details about how it would actually work in practice before I could land firmly on yes or no.

(B) not remove

Look, I might not agree with everything the guy says, but that's exactly why the library should keep it. If we start pulling books just because some people find them offensive or disagreeable, where does that end? 

A public library is supposed to have different viewpoints available. People can make up their own minds. I'd want my perspective represented if I wrote something, even if others disagreed with it.

I'd say **(B) routine** for the most part.

Don't get me wrong—there are moments that break things up. But honestly, a lot of my days follow a pretty predictable pattern. Work, home, the usual responsibilities. I think most people's lives are like that when you really think about it. It's not bad, just... the way things are. There's comfort in that, I guess, but sometimes I wonder what it'd be like if things were a bit more unpredictable.

(C) too much

Look, I get that we have legitimate international interests and responsibilities, but when I think about the problems here at home—infrastructure falling apart, healthcare costs, education funding gaps—it's hard to justify the amount we're sending overseas. I'm not saying we should cut it to zero, but we're stretched thin as it is. We need to take care of our own house first.

I'd say **(C) too much**.

Look, I understand we need a strong defense—that's not the question. But when you look at the actual numbers, the U.S. spends more on military than the next ten countries combined. Meanwhile, we've got infrastructure crumbling, healthcare costs through the roof, and schools that need funding.

I'm not saying cut it to nothing, but there's definitely room to trim without making us less safe. We could redirect some of that spending to problems that actually affect my daily life and my family's future. It feels like we've got our priorities backward sometimes.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, I see the problems in cities every time I visit—the infrastructure falling apart, homelessness, struggling schools. These aren't small issues you can fix on the cheap. It feels like we're constantly patching things up instead of actually addressing root causes. 

I get that money's tight and we can't solve everything at once, but we seem to be underfunding the real work that needs to happen. Whether it's mental health services, affordable housing, or public transit—these require serious investment. Right now it looks like we're just doing enough to keep things from completely falling apart, not enough to actually move forward.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, crime is a real problem in a lot of communities, and it seems like we're not getting ahead of it. You see the news stories—it's not getting better. If we were spending the right amount or enough, I feel like we'd see more progress by now. Whether it's police presence, prevention programs, or dealing with root causes like poverty and addiction, it feels underfunded to me. We talk about it being expensive, but the cost of *not* addressing crime—the victims, the lost productivity, the fear—that's expensive too.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, drug addiction is a massive public health crisis—it affects families, communities, jobs, everything. From what I see, we're treating it more like a criminal justice problem than a health problem, which costs way more in the long run anyway—prisons, emergency rooms, lost productivity.

If we invested more upfront in treatment, prevention, and mental health services, we'd probably save money and lives down the line. But right now it feels like we're just managing the crisis, not really solving it. That takes money we're not spending.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, I know education funding is already substantial, but when you see the state of a lot of schools—especially in lower-income areas—the crumbling buildings, outdated materials, teachers buying supplies out of pocket, larger class sizes... it's clear the money isn't getting where it needs to go or there just isn't enough of it.

Education is supposed to be our foundation. You get that wrong and everything else becomes harder to fix. Yeah, it's expensive, but underfunding it seems like we're cutting corners on something that should be a priority.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, I see the environmental issues we're dealing with—climate change, pollution, water quality. These problems aren't going away on their own, and they're only going to get more expensive to deal with down the road if we don't address them now. 

Yeah, environmental spending adds up, but the cost of *not* doing anything—damaged ecosystems, health problems, natural disasters—that's going to hurt us financially and otherwise in the long run. It seems like we're always playing catch-up instead of being proactive about it.

I'd say **(C) too much**.

Look, I understand people need help, and I'm not heartless about it. But from what I see, there's a lot of waste in these programs—bureaucracy, people gaming the system, fraud. We're throwing money at problems without actually solving them, and meanwhile my taxes keep going up.

That said, I know it's complicated. Some people genuinely need support. But I think we could be smarter about how we spend it rather than just spending more. Better oversight, tighter eligibility—that kind of thing.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, healthcare costs are high, sure, but that's not the same as spending too much on *improving* health. We've got people skipping medications because of costs, mental health services are stretched thin, and preventive care isn't reaching everyone who needs it. 

If we're paying more out of pocket and still not getting better outcomes compared to other countries, that suggests the money isn't being spent efficiently—but that's different from saying we're spending too much overall. We need more investment in actual health improvements, not just shuffling money around a broken system.

I'd say **(A) too little**.

Look, there are real disparities in education, housing, healthcare, and economic opportunity that have been documented pretty thoroughly. Whether you're talking about wealth gaps, homeownership rates, or educational resources—the numbers show significant inequities.

Now, I'm not naive about government spending or where money goes. But when I look at what's actually being invested in addressing these systemic issues versus the scope of the problems, it doesn't add up. Too much of it gets bogged down in bureaucracy or half-measures anyway.

That said, I recognize this is a complex question and reasonable people disagree on priorities and how to spend money effectively. But in terms of the amount dedicated to closing these gaps? I think we're underspending relative to the need.

(C) too much

Look, I get that space exploration can lead to technological spinoffs and all that, but when we've got real problems here on Earth—crumbling infrastructure, healthcare costs, education funding—it's hard to justify spending billions on rockets. Maybe if we had our house in order I'd feel differently, but right now it feels like a luxury we can't afford. We could do some space work at a smaller scale and redirect those resources where people actually need them day-to-day.

(B) no

I don't have any firearms in my home or garage.

I'd say **(D) independent (neither, no response)**.

Look, I've never really felt comfortable locking myself into one party or the other. I tend to look at issues individually rather than just following a party line. Some things the Democrats propose make sense to me, and some Republican ideas do too. The rest of the time, honestly? Both parties frustrate me in different ways. I find the whole "you have to pick a side" mentality exhausting.

I'd say **(D) moderate, middle of the road**.

Honestly, I don't fit neatly into one camp. I've got views that don't always align—I care about social issues and the environment, but I'm also practical about fiscal matters. I find myself agreeing with people on both sides depending on the specific issue. That's where I genuinely land.

I'd say **(B) there should be laws against the distribution of pornography to persons under 18**.

That feels like the most reasonable middle ground to me. Kids shouldn't have access to that material—they're not developmentally ready for it. But I also think consenting adults should be able to make their own choices. A blanket ban on all pornography seems like government overreach, but completely unregulated distribution puts minors at risk. Restricting it to adults seems like the practical balance.
raw_responses.selected_option: there should be laws against the distribution of pornography to persons under 18

(C) don't know

Honestly, I think that's the most truthful answer for me. I wasn't raised with strong religious convictions, so I don't have a framework that definitively tells me one way or the other. I've thought about it plenty—who hasn't?—but I can't say I *know* anything about what happens after we die. 

Some days I lean toward thinking consciousness just ends. Other times, I wonder if there's something more. But I try not to pretend certainty about things I can't actually verify. The not-knowing feels more authentic to me than picking a side just to have an answer.

(A) approve

Look, I think it makes sense. Public schools serve kids from all different backgrounds and religions—or no religion at all. A public school shouldn't be pushing any particular religious practice on students, especially when parents might have completely different beliefs at home.

If families want their kids learning the Lord's Prayer or Bible verses, that's what home and church are for. The school's job is to educate, not to promote religion. Keeping that separation just seems fair to everyone involved.

(D) not wrong at all

Look, I think consenting adults should be able to make their own choices about their relationships. People have different values and beliefs, sure, but I don't see how it's automatically wrong if two people care about each other and decide to be intimate before getting married. That's between them.

I'd vote for the second law (B).

Housing is a fundamental need, and discrimination in housing has a long, harmful history. Allowing people to be denied housing based on race perpetuates segregation and inequality. Fair housing protections ensure everyone has equal access to opportunities and communities, regardless of their race.

While I understand property ownership comes with certain rights, those rights shouldn't extend to discrimination in something as essential as housing. The broader community benefit of equal access outweighs an individual's preference to discriminate.

I'd say **(B) more or less satisfied**.

Look, we're managing okay. Bills are getting paid, we've got a roof over our heads, and we can put food on the table. But I won't pretend everything's perfect—groceries cost more than they used to, and I'm always a bit anxious about unexpected expenses. We're not struggling to survive, but we're not comfortable enough to stop worrying about money either. It's kind of that middle ground where you're doing alright, but you're definitely conscious of your budget.

I'd go with **(A) favor**.

Look, I think kids are going to learn about sex one way or another—better they get accurate, age-appropriate information from trained educators than from peers or the internet. Comprehensive sex ed covers not just the biology but also healthy relationships, consent, and safety, which seems important.

That said, I get that people have different values on this. I think parents should have some input, but opting out of factual health education altogether doesn't seem like the answer to me.

I'd say **(C) disagree**.

Look, I get that parenting is tough and kids can push your buttons. But from what I've seen and read, there are just more effective ways to handle discipline. Spanking might work in the moment, but it doesn't teach kids *why* their behavior was wrong. It teaches them to fear punishment, not to make better choices.

I think clear consequences, taking things away, time-outs—those kinds of things actually help kids understand cause and effect. Plus, there's research showing spanking can escalate into harsher treatment and doesn't lead to better long-term behavior.

That said, I'm not here to judge parents who've done it. Parenting's hard and everyone's doing their best. But if I'm being asked directly, I don't think it's necessary.

(A) yes, allowed to speak

Look, I might not agree with everything someone says, but people should have the right to express their views—even unpopular ones. That's kind of foundational to how things work. If we start shutting down speech we disagree with, where does it stop? 

I think free speech matters, even when it's controversial. Someone being against religion can make their case just like religious folks make theirs. That's how it should be.

(A) yes, allowed to speak

Look, I think people should be able to say what they believe, even if I disagree with them. That's what free speech is about. If we start shutting people up just because of their political views, where does that end? 

I'm not going to agree with a Communist—that's not the point. But preventing someone from speaking just because of their ideology doesn't sit right with me. It's more American than that.

I'd go with **(A) yes, allowed to speak** — though I want to be clear about my thinking here.

Allowing someone to speak isn't the same as agreeing with them or thinking their ideas are right. That speech would be harmful and wrong, full stop. But I believe in free speech principles, including for ideas I find repugnant.

The practical reason: once you start banning speech based on *what* is being said, you've opened a door that's hard to close. Who decides what's too offensive or false to allow? History shows that power gets abused.

Better approach: let him speak, and let people counter him directly. Bad ideas usually lose when exposed to pushback and evidence. Banning him might actually make him seem like a martyr to some people.

That said, there could be exceptions around *incitement to violence* — but just expressing a racist belief, however abhorrent, isn't quite the same thing.

(C) don't know

This is one of those questions where I genuinely feel torn. I can see the compassion in wanting to relieve someone's suffering, especially facing an incurable disease. But I also think about the complexity—like whether people in severe pain or depression can truly make a free choice, whether better palliative care might change things, and the different values people hold about life and death.

It's not something I feel confident taking a hard stance on either way. Different people's beliefs about this—religious, philosophical, personal—matter a lot here. I'd need to think through it more carefully before saying "yes" or "no" definitively.

(A) too high

Look, I work hard for my money, and a good chunk goes to federal taxes before I even see it. I understand we need taxes for infrastructure and services, but honestly, it feels like more than my fair share some years. I'm not sure exactly where all of it goes, and that makes it feel worse. If I could see clearer benefits or knew the money was being used efficiently, maybe I'd feel differently about it.

I'd go with **(C) depends**.

Look, I think it really comes down to context. Most people I interact with regularly—coworkers, neighbors, people in my community—I'd say they're generally trustworthy. But I'm not naive about it either. You've got to read the situation and the person.

If someone's a stranger or I don't know their track record, yeah, I'm cautious. That's just practical. But I also don't think you can go through life assuming everyone's out to get you—that seems exhausting and not realistic based on what I've actually experienced.

So it's not that most people can be trusted *universally*, but it's also not that you need to be suspicious of everyone all the time. It genuinely depends on who you're dealing with and what the stakes are.

I'd have to go with **(D) disagree somewhat**.

Look, I get the logic on the surface—different groups have faced discrimination and come through it. But the statement glosses over some real differences in how that discrimination worked out in practice.

Black Americans faced slavery that lasted centuries, then Jim Crow laws that were legally enforced well into my lifetime. That's not quite the same timeline as immigration-based discrimination, even though that was serious too. Plus, things like redlining and housing discrimination created wealth gaps that are harder to just "work through" in a generation or two.

I don't think that means special favors are necessarily the right answer either—that's complicated. But saying everyone should just do it the same way ignores that the starting positions weren't actually equal. That's why I can't fully agree with the statement.

I'd say **(B) almost always wrong**.

Look, I think infidelity violates the trust and commitment that marriage is built on. That's the foundation, you know? Breaking that has real consequences—it hurts people.

That said, I'm not going to sit here and say there are *never* circumstances where it's more complicated. Like, I can imagine edge cases—a couple in a dead marriage staying together for kids, maybe they've worked out some understanding. Or situations I'm not even thinking of.

But those would be rare exceptions. For the vast majority of marriages, that vow means something, and going outside it is fundamentally wrong.
